papers.title: Additive Fréchet Regression for Random Objects
papers.abstract: Regression analysis for complex data taking values in a general metric space has gained increasing attention in recent years, particularly in the context of Fréchet regression with Euclidean predictors $\mathbb{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$. However, local Fréchet regression, while more flexible than global Fréchet regression, suffers from the curse of dimensionality for the case of multivariate predictors. To address this issue while maintaining model flexibility, we introduce a framework of additive structured nonparametric regression when responses are situated in a general metric space. Overcoming the challenge of the lack of vector space structure in general metric spaces where the responses reside requires a novel approach that incorporates the additive structure via projection operators. This leads to a unified framework of additive regression for a wide range of response types, including one-dimensional distributions in Wasserstein space, network data represented by graph Laplacians and spherical data equipped with geodesic distances, among others. We establish pointwise and uniform consistency, including convergence rates, for the proposed additive Fréchet regression estimators, using smooth backfitting. The practical utility of this additive model is demonstrated through applications to brain connectivity network analysis using resting-state fMRI data and distributional physical activity data.

papers.title: BRUCE (Bayesian Rio Urban Climate Estimator): spatiotemporal interpolation of air temperature from heterogeneous sensor networks for operational heat monitoring
papers.abstract: Accurate characterization of intra-urban temperature variability is essential for heat-health surveillance, yet official monitoring networks are too sparse to resolve fine-scale gradients, particularly in Global South cities. We present BRUCE, a Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model, fitted with the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) and a Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE) spatial component, that fuses four heterogeneous temperature sources for Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: official weather stations, low-cost IoT sensors, citizen-science personal weather stations and ERA5-Land reanalysis. The model accounts for class- and station-specific measurement bias and estimates a continuous spatial field that evolves day to day through an autoregressive (AR1) structure. Fitted independently to nine monthly windows (January, June, November; 2023--2025), the elevation coefficient was significant in all windows and of consistent magnitude in eight ($-$1.08 to $-$1.38 \textdegree{}C per SD). In leave-region-out cross-validation against LCZ4r, accuracy was comparable (RMSE differences within station-level bootstrap uncertainty in all three windows), while BRUCE produced predictions at every held-out station, including those where LCZ4r is masked, and preserved finer-scale spatial structure than LCZ4r's discrete zone classification. Applied to 241 primary care territories, BRUCE's posterior exceedance probabilities allowed 96 to be classified with high confidence (model-based classifications), whereas a constant-width interval derived from LCZ4r cross-validation errors supported confident classification of none. The framework offers a statistically principled, operationally viable basis for intra-urban heat monitoring in data-heterogeneous settings.

papers.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
papers.abstract: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Risk-Based Hotspot Dynamics Assessment
papers.abstract: Analysis of hotspots often constitutes the final objective in application studies oriented to spatiotemporal risk assessment, particularly for risk mapping and as a helpful instrument for decision making, in diverse fields such as Ecology, Epidemiology, Environmental Sciences, Security, among others. The most primary form, common in practice, consists in identifying and depicting the areas where the magnitude of interest exceeds a certain critical threshold level. In this work, we introduce a wider, more general concept of `hotspot', associated with the extremal values of risk measures defined on different structural indicators of threshold exceedance sets, such as the exceedance area, the excess volume, etc. In particular, we propose a methodological approach based on empirical characterization of the indicator probability distributions from simulation conditional on the available observations, calculated at local resolution scales determined by sliding windows. Risk map generation is then supported by a proper conceptualization and formalization of a suitable family of risk conditional random fields (RCRFs), specified in terms of a set of input elements that can be viewed as flexible tuning parameters for practical implementation and application. For illustration, we consider an extension of a spatiotemporal diffusive blur-generated autoregressive model involving a dynamical spatial deformation. Evolutionary assessment of hotspots is then addressed under different scenarios, with reference to well-known quantile-based risk measures.

papers.title: Optimal Transport Rank Regression for Robust Multivariate-Response Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose optimal transport rank regression for robust multivariate-response mean regression. The proposed method maps residual distributions to the uniform measure on the unit ball and constructs its loss from the resulting optimal transport ranks. This construction exploits cross-response dependence to improve efficiency while preserving population Fisher consistency and orthogonal invariance. Beyond these population properties, we establish statistical guarantees for the proposed method in both linear and nonparametric regression. For linear models, we establish asymptotic normality, characterise robustness, and develop orthogonally invariant asymptotic inference. We derive a distribution-uniform lower bound on asymptotic efficiency relative to least-squares and demonstrate efficiency gains over coordinatewise methods under several heavy-tailed and contaminated distributions. For nonparametric regression, we establish non-asymptotic \(L^2(P)\) convergence rates and robustness guarantees modulo additive constants using deep neural networks under possibly asymmetric heavy-tailed noise, attaining the minimax-optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and inferential efficiency over coordinatewise and radial robust methods, alongside stability under orthogonal transformations of the responses. An oral microbiome application further shows that the proposed method identifies more associations that are significant in all examined orthonormal response representations compared with each competing method.

papers.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
papers.abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $β$-Hölder source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

papers.title: Interpreting the Morbidity Gap
papers.abstract: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study now reports the morbidity gap (MG), life expectancy minus healthy life expectancy, as an indicator in its own right. Writing MG as the expected cumulative rate of years lived with disability (YLDs) at the life-table age at death, we use stochastic dominance results to show what MG measures, how it responds to mortality and how it relates to the YLDs of the current population. We show the following. (a) A YLD profile gives an MG no larger than another's under every life table if and only if its cumulative YLD rate is nowhere higher. (b) With YLD rates fixed, lower mortality at every age widens MG, so that removing a risk factor that raises mortality reduces MG by less than its contribution to MG in GBD's risk factor attribution. (c) A family of results gives easily interpretable conditions on the age structure of the population for the crude YLD rate to be above or below the life-table YLD rate, which is MG divided by life expectancy, and these conditions change with population ageing. We illustrate the results for Singapore, where MG widened from 8.9 to 11.2 years between 1990 and 2023.

papers.title: Causal Effect Estimation Under Uncertain Statistical Surrogacy
papers.abstract: Surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal effect estimation, but such gains may depend on structural assumptions. One such assumption is statistical surrogacy, which requires the primary outcome to be conditionally independent of treatment given the surrogate and baseline covariates. We study causal effect estimation with multiple candidate surrogates of uncertain validity under statistical surrogacy, considering settings where the primary outcome is either fully observed or subject to missingness. We characterize the asymptotic efficiency differences between surrogate-assisted and benchmark estimators, examine the bias induced by violations of statistical surrogacy, and identify conditions under which incorporating surrogate information leads to efficiency gains or losses. To address uncertainty in surrogate validity, we propose Surrogate-assisted Adaptive Causal effect EStimation (SACES), a procedure that anchors estimation to a robust benchmark while adaptively selecting among a finite set of surrogate-assisted estimators using an estimated mean squared error criterion. SACES aims to leverage efficiency gains when statistical surrogacy holds while preserving consistency when the assumption is violated. Simulations demonstrate that SACES achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off across varying degrees of surrogacy violation. We illustrate the proposed methods using data from the ACTG 175 clinical trial to demonstrate how surrogate information can be adaptively incorporated into causal effect estimation.

papers.title: Elementwise Precision-weighted Compositional Data Analysis by Weighted Alternating Least Squares
papers.abstract: Logratio principal component is a multivariate method commonly used for exploring compositional data sets. This method is mostly used in an unweighted manner, employing the centred logratio transformation of the compositions. The smaller elements of a composition usually have a higher relative error, and can be downweighted using part-wise weighting. In this article we focus on weighting compositional data and propose elementwise precision weighting of compositions. This is particularly convenient for compositions with parts that fluctuate from rare to frequent; e.g. parts acting as traces in some samples, but being abundant in others. We suggest to weight in the logarithmic or logratio scale, with the inverse of the standard deviation of the logratio, the latter being estimated for each part of each composition separately. A weighted least squares algorithm is used for dimension reduction and compositional biplot construction. Several applications of elementwise precision weighting are described, using compositional datasets from genetics, archaeology and microbiomics that illustrate the power and advantages of a fully weighted compositional analysis.

papers.title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

papers.title: The long-term divergence exponent and the temporal structure of step-to-step perturbations: a simulation study in two passive walking models
papers.abstract: Purpose. Divergence exponents are used to assess the local dynamic stability of gait. Human experiments have related the long-term exponent ($λ_L$) to the complexity of gait fluctuations. Model studies used perturbations without controlled temporal structure. The question was whether $λ_L$ responds to the temporal structure of perturbations in walkers without neuromuscular control. Methods. Two passive walkers, M1 (pilot) and M2 (exploratory), received step-to-step perturbations of five amplitudes ($σ$) and nine temporal structures (ARFIMA parameter $d$), and human stride series of free and metronome walking. Results. At constant amplitude, $λ_L$ increased with $d$ in both models. It was higher with free series than with metronome series or with surrogates. It did not follow $σ$ in M1 and followed $σ$ in M2. Its double dissociation from the short-term exponent was supported in M1 only. In a descriptive analysis, the condition means of $λ_L$ correlated with the scaling exponent of the step durations ($r = 0.980$ in M1 and 0.906 in M2). Conclusion. In two passive walkers with fixed mechanics, $λ_L$ followed the temporal structure of the perturbations; its specificity depended on the model. This response supports the name attractor complexity index (ACI), proposed for $λ_L$ from human experiments.

papers.title: When Foundation Models Disagree: Representational Heterogeneity for Calibrated Uncertainty in Whole-Slide Image Classification
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.

papers.title: Fully Bayesian Benchmarking for Small Area Models with Count Data
papers.abstract: Small area estimates of counts are often required to conform exactly to reliable aggregates at a higher geographic level. Often the area-level model is specified on a transformed (nonlinear) scale such as a log scale. Specifying the small area model on the log-scale is common practice for positive responses. A prominent example is the production of the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE) by the US Census Bureau. When the model is specified in a transformed scale, the benchmarking constraints, which are linear in the area means, become nonlinear in terms of the model parameters. We develop a new class of priors for Bayesian small area models under strict external benchmarking constraints when the small area model is specified in a transformed scale, and the model parameters belong to a Riemannian manifold due to the nonlinear benchmarking constraints. The prior is fully supported on the constrained parameter set, the manifold defined by the benchmarking constraints, and thereby provides a proper constrained posterior that is also supported on the restricted set. This facilitates full Bayesian analysis of the problem without the requirement of post-hoc modification to the posterior to enforce the benchmarking constraints.

papers.title: Do Network Mechanisms in Science Vary Across Research Topics? Contextual Relational Hyperevent Models for Large-Scale Bibliometric Data
papers.abstract: Collaboration and citation networks in science are shaped by well-documented mechanisms such as preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation. Whether these mechanisms operate uniformly across research areas, however, is rarely tested, because statistical network models that estimate several mechanisms jointly are difficult to apply to large bibliometric data and to compare across subnetworks. We introduce contextual relational hyperevent models (C-RHEMs), which extend relational hyperevent models by allowing network effects to vary across research topics within a single model. C-RHEMs treat each publication as one event linking its authors to its references, accommodate reference lists spanning several topics, and scale to hundreds of thousands of publications on standard hardware. In a second step, meta-analysis and meta-regression quantify heterogeneity in topic-specific effects and relate it to topic characteristics. We illustrate the approach with about 590,000 oncology publications from the PubMed Knowledge Graph, assigned to 32 OpenAlex research topics. We find that preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation vary substantially across topics, with between-topic standard deviations of 30 to 70 percent of the corresponding pooled effects. Topic age, size, and gender composition account for between a third and two-thirds of this variation: older topics exhibit stronger preferential attachment, self-citation, and gender homophily, and topics with a higher share of male authors exhibit stronger self-citation. The results caution against treating network mechanisms estimated on pooled data as uniform, and C-RHEMs offer a scalable way to study how they differ across research areas.

papers.title: Measuring climate credibility? Talk, emissions, and corporate debt composition
papers.abstract: We examine whether a directional measure that compares emissions growth with earlier climate discussion is associated with corporate debt composition. The analysis links earnings-call climate language, LSEG/Refinitiv emissions, Capital IQ debt shares, RepRisk incidents, and accounting information for public firms over 2010--2021. The Emissions-to-Talk Index (ETI) is the central empirical measure, but we describe it literally rather than treating it as a general indicator of disclosure quality. In the baseline industry-and-year fixed-effect specification, a higher ETI is associated with a lower bank-debt share. The estimate falls by about four-fifths and is statistically insignificant when firm and year fixed effects are used on the same observations. It is also insignificant when the completed index is used to predict debt composition one calendar year later. Results based on the separate talk and emissions components, a ratio-free interaction, and complete talk--emissions categories lead to the same broad conclusion. Oster and Frank sensitivity calculations, alternative covariance estimates, exact year-sign bootstrap calculations, and leave-one-year-out estimates show that the contemporaneous result is sensitive to specification and inference. We also report exploratory comparisons by competition, financial health, opacity, and period; they do not show a consistent within-firm pattern. DealScan tests using unique facilities likewise show no common relation across facility incidence, spreads, maturity, security, and covenants. The evidence supports an association in the baseline industry-and-year specification, but not a causal claim that firms choose less bank debt to avoid monitoring or that lenders restrict credit because of the index.

papers.title: General Methodology for Asymptotically Balanced Multiple Tests
papers.abstract: In statistical applications, often more than one hypothesis is of interest and, thus, multiple testing problems occur naturally. To control the family-wise error rate, popular adjustment methods, like the Bonferroni and Holm correction, have been developed. However, these methods do not use the dependence structure of the test statistics. Consequently, they are conservative in most settings. To increase the power of the tests, the joint dependence structure of the test statistics can be incorporated for the construction of critical values, for example, by using resampling schemes as bootstrap procedures to approximate the joint distribution. This has already been applied in several contexts. In this work, we develop a very flexible and general theoretical foundation, which can be used to construct asymptotically balanced multiple tests that control the family-wise error rate in the strong sense. Additionally, we prove in the general setting that consistent resampling schemes satisfy the needed conditions.

papers.title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
papers.abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

papers.title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.

papers.title: Matrix elliptical sliced inverse regression: structured dimension reduction for heavy-tailed data
papers.abstract: Sliced inverse regression is widely used for sufficient dimension reduction, but existing matrix extensions that rely on covariance-based statistics can be unstable under heavy-tailed distributions. We propose matrix elliptical sliced inverse regression (MESIR) for estimating response-relevant row and column reduction subspaces under matrix elliptical distributions. We establish a mode-wise linearity relation linking the inverse regression curve to these subspaces through the corresponding scatter matrices. MESIR combines inverse-regression Kendall's tau matrices with eigenvalue-calibrated marginal Kendall's tau matrices. The calibration recovers the row and column scatter matrices needed to identify the reduction subspaces. Theoretically, we derive convergence rates for the calibrated marginal and inverse-regression estimators and establish subspace consistency under weak moment conditions, allowing the matrix dimensions and number of slices to diverge with the sample size. We further develop a consistent eigenvalue-ratio procedure for structural dimension selection and extend the method and theory to higher-order tensor predictors. Thorough simulation studies are conducted to show competitive performance under light tails and increasingly pronounced gains as the tails become heavier. Applications to COVID-19 CT images and radar target recognition demonstrate favorable empirical performance.

papers.title: The Statistical Cost of Second-Order Orthogonality
papers.abstract: Debiased machine learning removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation, but the remaining quadratic bias can invalidate inference when nuisance functions are hard to learn. Second-order orthogonal moments remove this bias at the cost of additional variance. We characterize this cost as the minimum variance of a correction that offsets the quadratic sensitivity of the moment to nuisance errors, and show that exact correction is possible only when this cost is finite. Because the cost varies across moments, the first-order efficient moment need not minimize total variance. We therefore choose the moment and its correction jointly, and derive the resulting minimum variance, a second-order analogue of the semiparametric efficiency bound. The optimal moment may trade first-order efficiency for a lower correction cost. In a binary choice logit model, it uses information beyond the conditional likelihood only in well-populated covariate cells; in difference-in-differences with continuous covariates, exact correction forgoes the efficiency gains from exclusion restrictions. In the partially linear model with continuous controls, the cost is infinite for every moment, so that only part of the bias can be removed. For such cases, we propose a data-driven adaptive rule that chooses how much bias to remove within a bound on variance inflation, and we show that inference remains valid after selection. In simulations for the partially linear model, the coverage of nominal 95\% intervals rises from 32--80\% to 94--97\% in all designs but a stress test.

papers.title: A Unified Unfolding and Slide-Vector Model for Asymmetric Dissimilarities via Clustered Lasso
papers.abstract: Asymmetric multidimensional scaling (AMDS) methods represent asymmetric dissimilarity data in a low-dimensional space. Existing approaches include the highly flexible unfolding model and the parsimonious slide-vector model. However, a highly flexible model is not necessarily optimal for adequately representing asymmetric relationships, and a model with an intermediate level of complexity may be more effective. In this study, we propose a new AMDS model that integrates the unfolding and slide-vector models by incorporating a clustered Lasso penalty. By fusing similar slide vectors, the proposed method can represent intermediate model structures and adjust model complexity according to the observed data. In numerical simulations, we compared the proposed method with existing methods by varying the number of groups, the number of objects, and the number of dimensions. The results demonstrated that the proposed method achieved high estimation accuracy across various asymmetric structures. Furthermore, in an application to cola brand-switching data, the proposed method achieved the highest accuracy in reproducing asymmetric relationships among the three methods compared and yielded a lower stress value than the slide-vector model. These findings suggest that adaptively adjusting model complexity may be effective for representing asymmetric relationships more accurately.

papers.title: Adaptive Tests of Pricing Restrictions with Observed and Latent Factors
papers.abstract: This paper develops a high-dimensional test for asset pricing models with observed and latent factors. The null hypothesis allows the intercepts from an observed-factor regression to be nonzero, provided that they lie in the latent factor loading space. We estimate the pricing errors in three steps: regress returns on the observed factors, extract latent factors from the lagged covariance structure of the regression residuals, and regress returns on both observed and estimated latent factors. The intercept from the final regression serves as the estimated pricing error. We construct Sum and Max tests based on the estimated pricing errors to detect diffuse and concentrated alternatives, respectively, and combine them using a Cauchy procedure. Under suitable regularity conditions, we establish the joint null distribution of the component statistics, their asymptotic independence, and their power against alternative hypotheses. We also propose a residual bootstrap and establish its first-order validity. Simulation studies examine the finite-sample performance of the tests under different pricing-error patterns and factor-number choices. An application to S\&P 500 stocks illustrates the use of the proposed framework in evaluating an observed-factor pricing model after latent-factor adjustment.

papers.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
papers.abstract: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Ab-initio cryo-EM reconstruction from moments of denoised images
papers.abstract: In single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), high-resolution three-dimensional (3-D) refinement requires a reliable ab-initio model to converge to the correct structure. Both refinement and existing ab-initio methods estimate the orientations of the particle images together with the 3-D structure, which can be slow for large and noisy datasets. We present a method of moments approach that bypasses orientation estimation and recovers a 3-D ab-initio model from the first three moments of denoised images. On experimental datasets, our method produces ab-initio models rapidly and successfully initializes high-resolution refinement. This is the first successful application of method-of-moments-based ab-initio modeling to experimental datasets without assuming a uniform distribution of orientations.

papers.title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
papers.abstract: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

papers.title: Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data
papers.abstract: When a fractional order improves the fit of an epidemic model, it is usually taken as evidence of memory. We ask whether the order of the Caputo susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model can actually be recovered from incidence data. If the transmission rate is allowed to vary freely in time, as in hybrid forecasting models, every admissible order, removal rate and initial count reproduces the data exactly. With constant transmission and exact data the order is identifiable in principle, but the dominant term of early linearized growth depends on only two parameter combinations: the growth rate r = (beta - gamma)^(1/alpha) and the amplitude beta*I0/alpha. What is left is transient, and it is limited. We prove that parameter sets sharing these two combinations give Poisson count distributions whose Kullback-Leibler divergence stays bounded no matter how long the linear phase is observed, and that the nonlinear model inherits this bound as the population grows. In simulations, wrong orders were rejected in at most 5% of replicates when the data ended two weeks or more before the epidemic peak, and in 95-100% once the peak was included; separation began only a few days before the peak. With mild overdispersion the order was identified only once about 60% of the population had been infected, and with stronger overdispersion not even then. Fits that the early data could not tell apart predicted peaks that differed by 75%, and plug-in forecasts that ignored parameter uncertainty were badly overconfident. Data generated without any memory produced fitted orders below one when transmission changed and when the fitted model was discretized in daily steps. In early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States, orders from 0.6 to 1 gave almost the same growth rate, whatever value we assumed for the removal rate.

papers.title: Structural Fine-Tuning under Economic Restrictions
papers.abstract: How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. The framework does not require a complete structural model; instead, it utilizes constraints based on economic knowledge, ranging from simple, ubiquitous assumptions to particular workhorse models. Theoretically, we characterize conditions when economic restrictions improve prediction over the original model and ordinary fine-tuning. Then, we illustrate the framework through a simulation exercise of a credit issuer's credit-limit decision following a Medicaid-style expansion in medical payments. Imposing restrictions based on eligibility, outstanding medical bills, cash flows, and group-level risk bounds, our framework lowers the root mean squared error of predicted risk by 28 to 39 percent and the issuer's policy regret by 3 to 10 percent relative to ordinary neuron gating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Single-fit inference for the realized prediction error of a logistic model with many predictors
papers.abstract: When independent validation data are unavailable, evaluating a fitted logistic model on new patients requires estimating prediction error and uncertainty. Evaluating the fit on training data is often optimistic. Bootstrap validation is widely used to correct this bias, but with many predictors, it can retain bias and yield unreliable confidence intervals. In this article, we study these limitations and develop single-fit estimation and inference without resampling. When the number of Gaussian predictors grows proportionally with sample size, we analyze unpenalized logistic models. We prove that standard bootstrap correction can have nonzero limiting bias even as the resample count grows and location-shifted intervals can have zero limiting coverage. Instead, we adjust the fitted scores to consistently estimate realized Brier and log losses. We account for common fitting and adjustment error to construct valid marginal intervals and joint regions. We also establish these single-fit estimation and inference guarantees for certain non-Gaussian designs in proportional dimensions. Under moderate dimension growth and possible misspecification with general predictors, we extend single-fit inference to ridge regularization and construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals for realized log loss. Simulations and analyses of hospital and diabetes datasets support our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

papers.title: Networked wealth and mortality in the Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System, 2009--2018
papers.abstract: Background. Though resources embedded in social networks appear to shape health, past studies have not assessed this relationship directly. Using data from Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System in South Africa, we examined the spillover effect of household wealth on mortality in the family network. Methods. We analysed cohort data from 2009 to 2018 to estimate the Average Total Effect (ATE) of household wealth on deaths, decomposing this into an Average Direct Effect (ADE) and Average Spillover Effect (ASE). We estimated these quantities separately for all deaths, deaths among children (<5 years old), premature deaths (among ages 15-59), and deaths among elders (60+). Results. Over the study period, 8750 individuals died. Overall, a one standard deviation increase in household wealth led to an ATE of -0.61% (95% CI: -0.74 to -0.48, P<0.001), an ADE of -0.53% (95% CI: -0.63 to -0.42, P<0.001) and an ASE of -0.08% (95% CI: -0.18 to 0.01, P=0.075). For premature mortality, these effect estimates were -0.37% (95% CI: -0.47 to -0.26, P<0.001), -0.29% (95% CI: -0.37 to -0.21, P<0.001), and -0.08% (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.00, P=0.038), respectively. Conclusions. Results provide evidence for the protective effect of household wealth on premature mortality across family relationships.

papers.title: Informative Local Average Treatment Effects Using Propensity Scores
papers.abstract: In instrumental variable (IV) models, comparisons of conditional local average treatment effects across covariates can mix effect heterogeneity in observed covariates with changes in the complier population, that is, those whose treatment responds to the instrument. Compliers at different covariate values may differ in unobserved characteristics that may also drive effect heterogeneity. We propose informative conditional local average treatment effects (ICLATEs), which condition on a subset of covariates of interest and on the treatment propensity scores under both values of a binary instrument. Fixing these scores holds constant the range of unobservables that drive treatment selection and thus compliance, while the composition of the covariates not conditioned on may change. Under conditional IV assumptions and suitable support conditions, we establish nonparametric identification and characterize the relationship of the ICLATEs to marginal treatment effects. We distinguish effect homogeneity in the unobservables driving treatment selection from effect homogeneity across excluded covariates. We clarify their roles in extrapolating complier effects to population effects and show that, jointly, they yield a testable implication even with a single binary instrument. For estimation, we combine cross-fitted machine learning of the nuisance functions with pooled local linear regression of doubly robust scores. Under undersmoothing and regularity conditions, we establish pointwise asymptotic normality, which a simulation study supports. As an empirical illustration, we apply the method to the Job Corps program to assess how the earnings effects of training participation vary with age.

papers.title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
papers.abstract: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2β_iβ_jσ_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.

papers.title: Network-Adaptive Instrumental Variables
papers.abstract: Three mechanisms generate endogeneity in regressions under interference. We address them by constructing network-adaptive instrumental variables (NIV) for a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights. Under network-conditional exclusion and information equivalence, the resulting instruments yield valid moments without knowing the true network. We establish joint identification of the structural mean coefficients and the network parameters, providing two sufficient routes. Then under additional covariance restrictions, we identify the disturbance spillover coefficient and the innovation variance. We develop NIV-GMM estimation, establish consistency and asymptotic normality, and give feasible inference and a test for mean network spillovers. Monte Carlo simulations examine their finite-sample performance.

papers.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Survival Regression with Time-Varying Covariates and Random Effects
papers.abstract: In longitudinal survival studies, biomarkers and treatments change across visits, their associations with event risk may be nonlinear and change over time, and subjects with identical measurements may differ in risk. Existing tree-ensemble survival models address these features separately: discrete-time formulations accommodate covariate updates without subject-specific random effects, and hazard-based ensembles with frailty take covariates as fixed at baseline. We propose Time-Varying Survival Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (TVSurvBART), a continuous-time hazard model combining a flexible baseline, a log-linear tree ensemble, and subject-specific random intercepts and slopes; covariates enter as predictable step processes, and interval-start time among the tree inputs lets effects change across visits. Integrated exposure offsets absorb the within-interval variation of the baseline and random slopes, so the tree leaves retain conjugate updates. Re-centering moves along likelihood-invariant directions and alternating centered and non-centered covariance updates address the resulting posterior dependence. In two simulation families, TVSurvBART's landmark predictions from held-out subjects' histories up to the landmark time have higher time-dependent AUC than the Cox, frailty Cox, and forest benchmarks in every setting and lower Brier scores in all but one comparison, although population-summary gains are not uniform. In the CARRA juvenile idiopathic arthritis registry, discrimination for recorded flares is similar to Cox regression, while a secondary interval-probability score favors TVSurvBART.

papers.title: The Scaled Dirichlet Distribution: Lauricella Representations and Estimation
papers.abstract: We derive explicit expressions for the mixed moments of the scaled Dirichlet distribution in terms of the Lauricella hypergeometric function of type $D$. The relationship with Carlson's multivariate $R$-function is stated, and the convergence conditions required for the series derivation are made explicit. The general expressions yield means, second moments and covariances, with Gauss and Appell hypergeometric representations in the bivariate and trivariate cases. Method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood formulations are presented, together with simulation summaries and an illustrative comparison of scaled Dirichlet and ordinary Dirichlet fits to compositional futures-return data.

papers.title: Improving External Prediction in New Clusters with Mixed-Effects Models: Implications for Multicenter Studies
papers.abstract: Prediction models developed from multicenter data are often applied to new centers. A linear mixed model (LMM) captures between-center heterogeneity through random effects. However, a new center's random effect is unknown, so the LMM predicts from fixed effects alone, as does a standard linear model (LM) that ignores clustering. The two models thus differ only in how fixed effects are estimated, and it is unclear whether the LMM predicts better. We decompose the prediction error in a new center into fixed-effect estimation error, between-center variation, and residual variation. Because the last two components are identical for both models, any LMM advantage must come from more precise fixed-effect estimates. In simulations across diverse designs and random-effect structures, the LMM generally achieved lower mean squared error than the LM. Relative gains increased with the number of predictors, between-center heterogeneity, and imbalance in center sizes, and decreased as training data grew. Modeling a random slope yielded additional gains that increased with between-center variation in the predictor effect. In a stress test using held-out eICU hospitals selected for strong outcome heterogeneity, a random-intercept LMM predicted ICU length of stay more accurately than an LM. These findings clarify the conditions under which mixed models can improve prediction in new centers and can inform model development for multicenter studies.

papers.title: Geometry, Local Minimax Risk, and the Limits of Sample Average Approximation in Linear Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We study how the local geometry of a linear stochastic optimization problem determines its statistical difficulty, measured by expected decision regret. The optimal local rate is governed by how fast the support function of the feasible set grows away from its linearization at the true mean; depending on the instance, it can be $n^{-1/2}$, $n^{-1}$, $n^{-2}$, or a non-power rate, and sample average approximation (SAA) attains these rates in a Gaussian mean model. At smooth instances, SAA also attains the classical sharp local minimax constant. We then allow the data distribution to vary in a Kullback--Leibler (KL) ball of radius proportional to $1/n$ around a reference distribution $P$. The exact local minimax limit of this benchmark, which may depend on $P$, coincides with that of a Gaussian model whose local parameter set is the covariance ellipsoid of $P$. A simple coordinatewise truncated SAA rule, which does not use $P$, attains the minimax rate, and at smooth instances its constant matches the minimax constant as the neighborhood radius grows. Ordinary SAA, in contrast, can have strictly suboptimal worst-case expected regret when the local rate is fast relative to the tails of $P$, because rare tail events then dominate the expectation. The results delineate when SAA is sharply optimal, rate-optimal, or statistically suboptimal, and quantify the local price of distributional robustness.

papers.title: On the Validity of Fisher Randomization Tests under the Weak Null
papers.abstract: Consider the problem of testing the Neyman weak null of no sample average treatment effect $H_{0N}:τ= 0$ in randomized experiments with binary outcomes. Although the Fisher Randomization Test (FRT) is typically justified under Fisher's sharp null of no individual treatment effect, we show that it is finite-sample-valid for the weak null $H_{0N}$ in three common combinations of study design and test statistic: 1) balanced completely randomized experiments with the difference-in-means test statistic, 2) matched pairs experiments with the same test statistic, and 3) balanced Bernoulli randomized experiments with the centered Horvitz-Thompson test statistic. As an immediate corollary, Fisher's exact test in a balanced completely randomized experiment is valid under the weak null, and so is McNemar's test in a matched pairs experiment. Similar results hold for the one-sided null $H_0:τ\leq 0$. Beyond balanced designs, we show that twice the one-sided FRT $p$-value with the same test statistics is valid under $H_{0N}$. In simulation experiments, the FRTs compare favorably to other exact procedures.

papers.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection
papers.abstract: The Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) monitors athletes for doping by comparing their biomarker readings against personalized reference ranges. These are estimated via the Bayesian ADAPTIVE model, which analyzes biomarkers separately and ignores their dependence. Building on a recently proposed copula-based multivariate extension of ADAPTIVE, this paper focuses on its computational aspects, introducing a fully joint MCMC algorithm and comparing it with a two-step Bayesian IFM estimator. Simulations show the two procedures perform comparably under a correctly specified copula, but exhibit a genuine trade-off under misspecification: the Bayesian IFM protects marginal inference, while the joint MCMC yields better-calibrated dependence estimates and is markedly faster. The two approaches are tested on a dataset containing ABP profiles of elite athletes, provided by NADO Italia, and collected as part of the project {\it Enhancing the methodological framework for doping detection: from univariate to multivariate testing analysis on Athlete Biological Passport profiles}. Both approaches achieve consistent classification performance, providing anti-doping organizations with two concrete inferential routes for adopting a multivariate ADAPTIVE model, along with guidance on the trade-offs between them.

papers.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
papers.abstract: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

papers.title: Inferring Neural Activity Changes under Recording Uncertainty with Transformers and Variational Inference
papers.abstract: A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

papers.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

papers.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
papers.abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

papers.title: Polycentrality in Urban Socioecological Systems: A Multilayer Analysis of Social Infrastructure in Iztapalapa, Mexico City
papers.abstract: The spatial distribution of infrastructure and activities, along with the networks and interactions that connect them, is key to understanding the relationship between urban form, function, and sustainability from a complex systems perspective. Within this dynamic relationship, the extent to which localized social infrastructure can reinforce existing functional centralities or create conditions for the emergence of new ones remains insufficiently understood. This study examines these relationships through the UTOPÍAS program in Iztapalapa, Mexico City, where 15 public social facilities have been established across a historically underserved urban territory. We develop a multilayer network framework integrating pedestrian infrastructure, GTFS-based public transport services, and UTOPÍAS as a target layer to assess multimodal connectivity, travel-time accessibility, and spatial coverage. These conditions are examined alongside indicators of local economic centrality (PCI and wPCI) to investigate how infrastructure interdependencies relate to the functional organization of urban space. The analysis reveals spatial heterogeneity in multimodal accessibility and differences in the integration of UTOPÍAS with existing transport networks. By relating these patterns to pre-existing economic centralities, we examine whether distributed social infrastructure may reinforce established functional centers or create conditions favorable to emerging centralities, without assuming that spatial decentralization necessarily produces polycentrality. The findings contribute a relational, data-driven approach to understanding how social infrastructure and mobility shape urban functions, emphasizing accessibility and territorial integration as critical conditions for more equitable and sustainable urban development.

papers.title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
papers.abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

papers.title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
papers.abstract: Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

papers.title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
papers.abstract: Conventional network representations inferred from multivariate time series describe statistical relationships between pairs of components, even when the underlying dynamics involve group interactions that cannot be represented by pairwise interactions alone. Several multivariate information-theoretic measures have been proposed to characterise dependence beyond pairs. However, due to a lack of systems with known generating mechanisms, these measures have not been carefully validated or compared for empirical use. To address this, we here introduce a generative model of stochastic network dynamics with pairwise and higher-order interactions specified by the user. The higher-order interactions are represented by directed hyperedges, and the model provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic measures. Removing only the higher-order term gives a pairwise-only reference. The experiments test whether a measure detects changes induced by the higher-order term relative to this reference and recovers the participating nodes and their source-target roles. A separate experiment tests discrimination between a product coupling and a specified nonlinear pairwise control, with equal root-mean-square coupling magnitude under the pairwise-only reference. Several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions across the tested network topologies and coupling functions. In the separate discrimination experiment, the measures also separated the product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control. Recovery, however, became harder as the number of candidate interactions grew. The framework therefore provides a testbed where the link between higher-order signatures and mechanisms can be tested, rather than assumed, before measures are applied to empirical data.

papers.title: A Local False Discovery Rate Framework for Compound p-values
papers.abstract: Compound p-values relax individual p-value validity to an average condition across the null hypotheses. This flexibility, however, need not protect particular rejections, especially when paired with an average error criterion such as the false discovery rate (FDR). In this work, we introduce "density-compound p-values," a concept that connects compound p-values and the frequentist local FDR paradigm. Under independence, we establish boundary FDR (bFDR) guarantees for the support-line (SL) procedure, with nominal-level control for weighted and compound-e-weighted p-values. For general density-compound p-values, our bounds depend on a tractable null-distribution parameter, and we show that without further restrictions on this parameter, the bFDR can substantially exceed its nominal level. Our theory extends to discrete compound p-values constructed by pooling permutation tests. Applications illustrate the method in low-resolution testing problems, where individually valid permutation p-values are too coarse to yield discoveries after multiplicity correction.

papers.title: Advancing mixed-effects random forests for predictions based on multi-cohort data
papers.abstract: Pooling longitudinal cohorts can extend age coverage and improve long-term health predictions, but cohort heterogeneity complicate estimation and prediction. Mixed-effects machine learning (ME-ML) combines flexible machine learning methods with mixed-effect models to account for correlated observations, yet these ME-ML methods are limited in their applicability in complex settings such as multi-cohort data. We propose a multi-cohort mixed-effects random forest (MERFmulti-cohort) for improving predictions of individual health trajectories beyond the observed period. The method extends standard MERF through (i) better separation of population-level and subject-specific variation, (ii) flexibility in correcting systematic discrepancies in fixed-effects estimates to improve covariance parameter estimation, and (iii) flexible specification of random-effects and residual variance-covariance structures. We evaluate MERFmulti-cohort against linear regression, linear mixed models, random forests, and standard MERF in simulations and four real-data scenarios predicting BMI z-scores in children and adolescents. In simulations, MERFmulti-cohort improves covariance parameter estimation across several covariance structures while achieving prediction accuracy comparable to standard MERF. Predictive gains are most obvious when residual variances vary across study waves. In real-data applications, MERFmulti-cohort improves predictive accuracy relative to MERF by flexibly capturing complex patterns and accommodating cohort heterogeneity. Pooling similar cohorts covering extended age coverage can improve future individual-level predictions if the heterogeneity in multi-cohort data is adequately accounted for.

papers.title: FRCI: An R Package for fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals
papers.abstract: Fuzzy confidence intervals provide a flexible framework for statistical inference by representing uncertainty through membership functions rather than fixed interval endpoints. Closely related to randomized confidence intervals, they offer an alternative approach for dealing with the conservativeness that frequently arises in discrete statistical models. Despite their attractive theoretical properties, the practical use of fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals has been limited by the lack of readily available software implementations. This paper introduces FRCI (Fuzzy and Randomized Confidence Intervals), an R package available on CRAN for constructing and visualizing fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals. The package implements confidence interval procedures for parameters of the normal, Bernoulli/binomial, and Poisson distributions, including a recently proposed method based on reference value choice, Geyer-Meeden, Agresti-Coull, and score methods. The main function computes the membership function associated with a selected confidence interval procedure, while dedicated graphical tools facilitate visualization and comparison of fuzzy confidence intervals. We describe the statistical background underlying the implemented methods, discuss the package design, and illustrate its use through several examples. The FRCI package provides researchers, practitioners, and students with an accessible and unified environment for the study and application of fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals.

papers.title: Design-Based Inference for Fuzzy Difference-in-Differences
papers.abstract: I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers' effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. I derive the conditions under which the estimand holds a clear causal interpretation. The conditions are weaker than parallel trends in both outcomes and treatments. We propose an Anderson--Rubin-type test with a conservative Neyman variance that remains valid under weak first stages, a sensitivity analysis for the complier effect, and estimators for designs with known assignment probabilities. An application to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment illustrates the results.
